title: What the World Fears of a Lame-Duck Trump
author: Daniel W. Drezner
text: Podcast What the World Fears of a Lame-Duck TrumpA Conversation with Daniel W. Drezner and Elizabeth N. Saunders Published on November 19, 2026 Play Listen to the Episode 65 minutes 00:00 / 1:05:17 0.5×1×1.25×1.5×2× MP3 Close audio player Print Print this article Save Sign in and save to read later Close Share What the World Fears of a Lame-Duck Trump A Conversation with Daniel W. Saunders Share in email Share on Facebook Share on X Share on LinkedIn Article link: https://www.foreignaffairs.com/podcasts/what-world-fears-lame-duck-trumphttps://www.foreignaffairs.com/podcasts/what-world-fears-lame-duck-trump Request reprint permissions here.Episode Details Donald Trump’s second-term foreign policy has brought some continuity, with the president acting on long-standing fixations on trade and allies and more. It’s also brought some surprises, especially when it comes to the use of military force.Now, Trump is entering the lame-duck period of his presidency. And with larger-than-expected midterm wins, Democrats are making grand promises about ending the war in Iran, exposing globe-spanning corruption, and much else.In a recent article for Foreign Affairs, Daniel Drezner, a professor of international politics at Tufts, and Elizabeth Saunders, a professor of political science at Columbia, considered what Trump can, and cannot, achieve internationally in the next two years. Dan Kurtz-Phelan spoke with them on Wednesday, November 18, about the possible consequences of Trump’s lame-duck foreign policy—and about the debates within both parties about what should come next.Sources:“The Dangers of a Lame-Duck Trump” by Daniel W. Drezner and Elizabeth N. Saunders“Trump’s Year of Anarchy” by Daniel W. Drezner and Elizabeth N. Saunders“The End of American Exceptionalism” by Daniel W. Drezner“Politics Can’t Stop at the Water’s Edge” by Elizabeth N. Saunders“The Unconstrained Presidency” by James Goldgeier and Elizabeth N. Saunders“The End of Hypocrisy” by Henry Farrell and Martha FinnemoreThis episode of The Foreign Affairs Interview was produced by Adelaide Parker and Kanishk Tharoor, with audio engineering by Todd Yeager and original music by Robin Hilton. Special thanks to Irina Hogan.This is a rough transcript of the conversation. Please consult the underlying audio prior to citation.DAN KURTZ-PHELANDan, Elizabeth, thank you for doing this.DANIEL DREZNERThanks for having us.ELIZABETH SAUNDERSPleasure to be here.DAN KURTZ-PHELANWe’re having this conversation not quite at the halfway mark of Trump’s second term. You two have written compellingly, both together and separately, about the Trump foreign policy and the broader foreign policy debate surrounding it. To start, I’m interested in how the foreign policy that has actually been carried out by this administration has and has not fit with your expectations of it and what that tells us about what we might see over the next couple of years. Elizabeth, to start with you, you argued in a piece in 2024 that Trump’s actions this year are far easier to predict than they were in 2016. Quoting you here, “the candidate who wanted to be the ‘madman’ and loved the idea of keeping other countries guessing has become a politician with a pretty predictable agenda.” In what ways has the second term foreign policy aligned with your prediction of predictability and where has it surprised you?ELIZABETH SAUNDERSWell, on the one hand, you could say that he’s blown that analysis out of the water because he’s been quite unpredictable and he’s done some things that are really... Even I didn’t think he would ever do. I didn’t think he would attack Venezuela. I didn’t think he would attack Iran. I was totally wrong about that. So if you think about it in terms of a geopolitical VIX volatility, he is the number one most... He gets the highest VIX of any president ever, and even compared to his first term. So in that sense, he has been unpredictable.On the other hand, he is still adhering to his guiding lights of foreign policy, his north star, which as originally Tom Wright wrote a year before Trump got elected in 2016, he’s got three basic principles that he never has deviated from. He doesn’t like multilateral trade agreements, he doesn’t like alliances, and he really loves authoritarian leaders. And with his bear hugs with Xi this morning in China, he’s sticking to that script, and much of his foreign policy can be boiled down to those three things. I think that the biggest addition in the second term has been corruption, which guardrails maybe prevented him from trying too much of in the first term, but the guardrails are gone. So I think what we have is more of the same Trump agenda unleashed more than a real wandering away from his central principles. He believed those three things long ago and he still does, and that’s what guides him.DAN KURTZ-PHELANDan, you published a piece in Foreign Affairs the day after the election in 2024, and you argued in that piece that Trump will “navigate world politics with greater confidence this time around. Whether he will have any better luck bending the world to his ‘America first’ brand is another question entirely.” Looking at the reactions to Trump in the international system, there are some places where he has had more success than I would’ve guessed bending others to his will, and others where you’ve seen greater pushback, especially over time. How do you understand that set of reactions and what does that tell us about the nature of power and the views of the United States under Trump?DANIEL DREZNERI think it’s pretty easy to split how Trump has succeeded versus how he hasn’t. He’s largely had success with mostly asymmetrically dependent allies. So in the Americas, in the Western hemisphere, for example, he’s largely gotten Mexico to comply with him when it comes to questions of migration. The administration has taken an active role in trying to influence elections in Latin America, trying to install more conservative populists in power, and again, by and large has been successful. In places like Argentina, for example, there was the loan to Javier Milei to try to bolster his party’s standing, and at least that did work in the short term. There have been favorable elections for Trump in Colombia, and of course there was the Venezuela operation.Similarly, in Europe, I think it’s safe to say that the European Union probably didn’t put up quite as much of a fight when it came to the trade war or the Liberation Day tariffs as you might’ve expected or potentially as they were capable of. They also didn’t necessarily concede all that much either, so I don’t want to over-exaggerate what Trump succeeded. And there have been a couple of minor economic security agreements signed with countries in the Southeast Asian region.Where he has met less success, I think is a function of two things. First, with larger countries, he hasn’t really been able to pressure all that much. So the fact that Canada has resisted. I mean, admittedly, Canada is smaller than the United States, but he has managed to strongly bolster. He’s been Mark Carney’s greatest gift. It’s worth remembering that prior to Trump’s election in 2024, all the expectations were for conservatives to win that election. Carney comes out of nowhere, and in resisting Trump’s trade war has genuinely unified the Canadian political establishment behind him. Similarly, with Brazil, Lula has been able to push back on Trump and was able to thwart Bolsonaro’s son from winning the most recent election.But also it is most particularly adversaries in the United States where Trump has had almost no effect whatsoever. He was able to push out Maduro, absolutely, but whether it was trying to get Russia to come to some kind of accommodation in the war with Ukraine, Trump has bent over backwards trying to be nice to Putin and hasn’t really accomplished anything. And he also misread Ukraine, I would add, the most infamous Oval Office meeting in which he told Zelensky he doesn’t have the cards, and it turns out he got a lot more cards than Trump realized. Similarly, the prosecution of the war with Iran has demonstrated that he can’t necessarily bomb his way to victory when dealing with an actual country.The most prominent failure I think is China, where he launched a big trade war in 2025 consistent with what he was doing in his first term, and China retaliated and Trump folded like a cheap suit. Essentially, the Chinese were prepared for this. They reciprocated with higher tariffs. They also imposed a rare earth embargo, embargoed magnets. Trump quickly, not only caved, but also made it clear that he didn’t want to roil Sino-American relations from then on, and that has been the modus operandi for the last 16 months.DAN KURTZ-PHELANThe other change that has surpassed what I would’ve guessed is the extent to which allies and others have raised their own defense spending, and that has as much to do with anxiety about Trump and the U.S. as it does about pressure, but that has been a market change.DANIEL DREZNERThat’s been an undeniable... I mean, Trump could count that as a success, particularly on the European side where they’ve committed to spending, I think, 3.5 percent of GDP on defense and five percent on defense and defense-related things. That is definitely an area where it happened. But as you point out, that’s as much due to hedging against the United States as it is acceding to Trump’s demands.ELIZABETH SAUNDERSI would just say also, apropos of both your points about allies and about adversaries, Trump is a terrible wielder of power. He inherited a decent economy, a pretty good economy, and the world’s most powerful military, and whatever you think about U.S.-China competition, the United States is still the most powerful country in the world, and he has used power against allies in a way that is wasteful. It’s not sustainable for him to put this kind of pressure on Canada and indefinitely antagonize our nearest neighbor with whom our economies are totally intertwined. The defense spending, okay, but the problem is he doesn’t ever seem to think about what the allies and adversaries are thinking, that they have agency. One reason why the United States has tolerated the lower level of defense spending for so long is because what it gets out of it, which is it gets to boss the Europeans around, and that’s what you lose when they become an independent military force, and presidents have thought that that trade-off was worth it.With China and Russia, he hasn’t actually used any of the real leverage that he could have used. I think tallying up wins and losses is not the whole story. I mean, it’s almost like the stockpiles of munitions that he’s wasted in Iran. He’s taken a lot of people out, he’s caused a lot of damage, but in the long term, he has severely weakened U.S. power, and I think he doesn’t understand the concept of strategic restraint. He doesn’t understand the concept that the adversary has agency in domestic politics, and Canada is a great example of that. You attack them and you get a unified country willing to line up behind Mark Carney.DANIEL DREZNERI would add that the one through line between Trump’s first term and his second term, it’s actually been on more in display in his second term, is Trump is a radically impatient leader. That’s the other thing to realize. He wants instant results and he wants instant feedback, which is why he’s always so sensitive to the markets, but it explains a lot of what he’s done over the last 20 months, which is he imposed the Liberation Day tariffs using the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, which the Supreme Court eventually ruled was unconstitutional, and he had other tariff powers he could have used, but that would’ve taken time and he wanted immediate results. I think it also explains Trump’s attraction to military force over the last year and change, which is he can order the military to do something and they will do it. And so it is an immediate feedback effect that he clearly likes.Obviously, the combination of what happened, the joint strike against Iran with Israel in 2025, plus the Venezuela operation, plus I suppose the Caribbean boat strikes, probably reaffirmed for him the notion that he could have the military do anything and it would lead to a quick victory, which explains why we’re in the quagmire in the Persian Gulf right now.ELIZABETH SAUNDERSYeah, he’s impatient without wanting to do any work, right? I know people in life who do a ton of work and are also impatient when they get to the conference or whatever and they want results, but they put in their work and he just does not do diplomatic legwork, staff work. He doesn’t care about any of it.DAN KURTZ-PHELANElizabeth, your point about power makes me think of the work you’ve done in our pages and elsewhere on the imperial presidency and the extent of presidential power. I think this somewhat cuts against the critique of Trump’s use of power you’re applying to the international stage in that he seems very good at accumulating power domestically, whether it’s put to effective ends is another question, but just the extent to which he has defied norms and dismantled constraints on his power. This has been, as you’ve written for us, a kind of one-way ratchet over for many, many decades. How much has this changed the picture of the imperial presidency that you’ve studied, again, going back before Trump, and to what extent do you anticipate a backlash to this in Congress? In a piece you read early in the Trump administration noted that this kind of crisis often is the only thing that precipitates real congressional action on putting instruments back in place. So as you look at this picture, both how much has this changed and what do you expect in terms of reaction to that?ELIZABETH SAUNDERSWell, I think on the one hand, he is the culmination of a very long trend, right? So presidents have been accumulating more and more power, the executive branch, with Congress willingly handing it over since the end of World War II. And the beginning of that was really the growth of the national security state in the nuclear age, the complexity of trying to manage it was something Congress felt was best done in the executive branch. And that really sort of took off in a dramatic way after 9/11. So the PATRIOT Act and many other congressional grants of executive authority and national security and then the development of drones. So by the time Trump took office the first time, the presidency was already immensely powerful. Even Barack Obama who ran... People forget he ran in 2008 on reforming executive power, Bush had too much executive power. He didn’t do anything to stop the growth of executive power.So I think that’s the sort of long-term trend and what Trump has done to some extent in the first term and dramatically in the second term is just snatch up all the remaining bits of executive power that norms had essentially kept out of the president’s hands. And so using emergency powers, breaking all the norms of corruption, using the military in ways... I think the Caribbean boat strikes are the most clear example of ways that basically are borderline murder. Not borderline, they are murder.DANIEL DREZNERYeah, I was going to say they’re not very borderline.ELIZABETH SAUNDERSRight. So norms don’t constrain Trump from doing anything, and so in the absence of advisors that were around in the first term and weren’t loyal to him and felt that they needed to constrain his worst impulses, there are no constraints left on him now. And I have said in Foreign Affairs that this means we have the foreign policy of a personalist dictatorship. And even with a Democratic Congress, there’s very little that Congress can do to restrain the day-to-day foreign policy of a president who doesn’t respect norms. And I think we will have a personalist foreign policy till the end of Trump’s term. As to what can be done about it, Congress has to decide if it wants to get back in the business of being a player in national security and foreign policy. I think that’s a fundamental question. It will depend a lot on the health of the Republican Party, which is frankly the unhealthy party in terms of policy. I’ve also written that I think it would be better if we had more politics where we debated this.It’s not healthy to not have two parties focused on the debates of national security. The Nvidia story is a great example. If you want to have a serious debate about whether we should be selling chips to China on national security grounds, that was the Jensen Huang position, or whether you should restrict them, reasonable people can disagree about that, and you want political parties to have that debate both in secret, closed door classified settings, and also to the extent it can be done in public. These are huge national concerns, but the way that Trump operates and the way the Republican Party has gone along with him, we don’t have that. We have Jensen Huang whose conduct has discredited that pull of the debate, and we have the Democrats or those who many China hawks in the Republican Party want to also restrict chips.I think one concrete thing that could be done if leadership in Congress is willing to think about it is to reform the committee system, because one thing that I think we’re missing is the era of the very strong committee chairman who have an interest, not just for their party, but for themselves in having a very strong reputation on national security and foreign policy. Also, probably healthcare, but that’s not what we’re here to talk about, right?DAN KURTZ-PHELANIn the golden age of a strong committee chair, you would imagine a Senate Armed Services or Senate Foreign Relations Committee chair who sees, I suppose, himself in that golden age, but himself or herself now as an independent power with their own views and their own ability to yield an agenda and shape the president’s agenda. That’s the ideal version too?ELIZABETH SAUNDERSYes, I think that’s exactly right. In the Carter era, if you wanted to do anything on nuclear anything, you had to go through Sam Nunn. And the mechanism, as many scholars of Congress, including CFR’s Jim Lindsay have written, the mechanism that Congress really exerts its power through is not passing bills, it’s the mechanism of anticipated reactions, right? You need the president to be thinking, “I’m thinking about doing this policy or this action. How is the person in Congress who knows about this going to react?” And just thinking about that can cast a shadow over presidential decision-making and exert constraint. And that is a very powerful mechanism, but it depends on somebody being in the building in Congress whose reaction can be anticipated.DAN KURTZ-PHELANSo just to make sure I understand, so Senator Sam Nunn, Democratic Senator from Georgia, and the Carter administration. If Jimmy Carter, president from the same party, did not consult him on a nuclear policy question, Nunn would then punish him by rejecting funding for other things or not confirming nominees, using whatever power he has to punish him, even if he can’t change the original policy?ELIZABETH SAUNDERSYeah, and it goes both ways. Certainly, Nunn has tools available to him or the mythical powerful committee chair has tools to impose political costs on the president. That’s the insider’s game that I talk about in my most recent book. But it’s also that if you can get Sam Nunn, you bring along all the other members of Congress who don’t specialize in nuclear things, who’ve specialized in healthcare or appropriations or whatever the issue is, and who look to Sam Nunn for guidance on the nuclear questions. So it’s not just the cost, it’s also the benefits of bringing someone like that along. Now, there are plenty of critiques one can make of the all powerful committee chair. Fulbright was the chair of Senate Foreign Relations for a long time and abetted the Vietnam War, partly because of his relationship with Lyndon Johnson, later turned on him though. No system is perfect. There are trade-offs, and having one person with strong views in power for too long can be very detrimental.On the other hand, I think having no policy expertise in Congress and having policy completely divorced from politics, everything is just done on party lines and nobody has the incentive to invest in expertise, that is a real problem. The pendulum has swung too far, I think, in favor of centralized leadership decision-making on all of these issues, complex bills and so forth, but also just the party line and having more powerful committee chairs I think would help with that a lot.DAN KURTZ-PHELANDan, you wrote a piece, as I mentioned, right after the election, and the central point of that was about what you call the end of American exceptionalism. Exceptionalism tends to elicit eye rolls from skeptics of American foreign policy on both left and right. What do you mean by exceptionalism when you talk about it, and to what extent has that in fact changed in Trump’s second term, how durable it changes that?DANIEL DREZNERSure. The idea of American exceptionalism is that America’s unique history, namely the lack of having a socialist party, the lack of having any sort of feudal structure prior to independence, and the sort of ideals originally articulated in the Declaration of Independence meant that once the United States entered the global stage, it did have a core set of democratic values that it did not just think were useful domestically, but also wanted the rest of the world to embrace. So this, in the modern sense, got translated into the idea of democracy promotion and human rights promotion. Now, there was always some element of hypocrisy contained within this. I don’t want to say that the U.S. has always been in favor of this, and all you have to do is look at the longstanding relationship between the United States and Saudi Arabia to realize that that’s not the case.ELIZABETH SAUNDERSOr slavery.DANIEL DREZNEROr slavery. Yes, that’s a good point. Good point on that slavery thing, Elizabeth. But nonetheless, I think there are two aspects of this that are important. The first is that you could argue, I believe circa Martin Luther King, that the arc of history bends towards justice, the arc of American history bent towards a greater embrace of democracy and human rights domestically and internationally. So this had become a somewhat important component of U.S. foreign policy. And as an ideal, I think it was something that the United States did in the belief of articulating American values overseas. It allowed the United States to do good and do well, which is to say that the belief that if other countries are democracies, if other countries embrace human rights, that creates a world that is more consistent with U.S. interests. And even from a strategic perspective, Joe Nye’s articulation of soft power, one of the components of that is values that are attractive to others, and human rights and democracy are pretty attractive globally.It would be safe to say that this is also saying that Donald Trump is categorically rejected. He’s done so throughout his entire political career. We are now in the absurd situation where, for example, Secretary of State Marco Rubio recently had to scold Nobel Peace Prize winner Maria Machado for when she returned to Venezuela, how dare you think about having a large demonstration? Don’t think you can demonstrate your way to electoral victory, which is super odd given that it was the opposite of the advice that Rubio and others gave to Iranians late December and early January of this year.But it shows that, I’m not sure the United States when it comes to this issue is in any way now seen as a beacon of democracy. As to how permanent this is, that remains to be seen. You can argue that the midterm elections in and of themselves represent a pretty strong rebuke of this, and also, by the way, send a powerful signal to the rest of the world that Trump is term-limited and he is in a weaker position now than at any time in either term of his presidency in terms of what he’s going to be able to do. He’s not going to be able to get congressional cooperation. There is likely to be significant oversight, so that in and of itself is a good thing.As to whether or not post-Trump, you will see the return of these kinds of values, it’s honestly an interesting question, and I think it goes back to Elizabeth’s point about there’s going to need to be a more widespread debate about this, not just I think between the parties, but also within the parties. I do suspect that the 2028 presidential primaries are going to be a good venue for this to happen. I mean, the one thing the midterms have demonstrated is that it is going to be a wide open primary on both sides of the aisle, and I suspect you’re going to see different articulations of foreign policy values and interests in those debates. Foreign policy tends to, I think, in a weird way, matter a little more during a primary because it’s one of the few areas where they can disagree while still being members of the same party. They’re not going to disagree about things like Medicare expansion or tax cutting, depending upon which party you’re talking about, but in foreign policy, they can actually evince different points of view.ELIZABETH SAUNDERSI think it’s also important to note apropos of Dan’s points, what Dan is describing is hypocrisy as almost like a strategic resource, and this goes to one of my-DANIEL DREZNERA lubricant, a social lubricant as you would.ELIZABETH SAUNDERSYes. All the time favorite Foreign Affairs pieces of recent vintage that neither of us wrote by Henry Farrell and-DANIEL DREZNERMarty Finnemore.ELIZABETH SAUNDERSMarty Finnemore, both former colleagues of mine who are just... I’ve always wished this had been my idea, but it’s one of those like, “Darn, I wish I wrote that.” And I teach it to students and it’s very eye-opening for them. This idea that the United States, from the beginning, a country that at its founding had slavery built into its constitution and has, from time immemorial, really exhorted other countries to do what it has not yet even finished doing, completing a transition to democracy in all its borders. Somebody made the argument the South has never really gone that far, protecting human rights, et cetera. On the other hand, one of the things you get when you’re a great power is the ability to act hypocritically, and this sounds so cynical, but it is in fact a strategic resource. We all talk about our friends behind their backs, but you don’t want that stuff leaking out into the open. And being socially adept is sort of keeping that out of social media or not talking about it too loudly in the hallway or whatever it is.Donald Trump has none of those skills, and he also doesn’t believe in it. He just wants to say out loud whatever is... He says the quiet part out loud all the time. And again, one thing that... I do think the midterms are a very strong rebuke, but one thing I do worry about is all of that depends a lot on trust and on people being willing to see the benefits of going along with the public facing kind of democracy promotion and human rights is outweighing all the times the United States violates those very principles. For a long time, that bet was a good one for most of the rest of the world. I don’t know how you go from this back to a situation in which you can credibly promote democracy and human rights and get the soft power benefits of that after two terms of Donald Trump. It’s hard to imagine.DAN KURTZ-PHELANIt is worth noting that that piece, which I agree is fantastic, was published in 2013 in Barack Obama’s second term, which could be taken as evidence that exceptionalism was always a lie or more of a lie than Dan is admitting.ELIZABETH SAUNDERSYeah, and they were reacting to the Snowden leaks, which is the reason why when I teach it, I talk about, “you can talk about your friends behind their back, but you can’t put it on social media.” If they find out about it, it’s icky, even though we all know that our friends talk about us behind our backs. So some of the stuff like spying on our allies, everybody kind of knows that goes on, but you don’t really want to see it in print, and it stings in a different way when you hear what your friends said about you, even though you know they talk about you behind their back. So there are other contributors to the decline, technology, the ability of one person to get all that stuff on a thumb drive and put it on the Internet. But I think Donald Trump has gone further than... Again, his geopolitical VIX is so high, no other president would ever want to damage that resource.DANIEL DREZNERI would add here that it’s true. The thing about Donald Trump is there’s not a ton of hypocrisy. There’s a lot of contradictions, but he just says whatever comes to him. I think the difference is that when you’ve had past presidents or past Secretary of State or what have you, there was a recognition that while they would make the occasional real politic move, I think there was also a belief that at their core, they actually did care about these values and it was a part of what they wanted to do. And in terms of soft power, for example, think about the WikiLeaks revelations, which I think in a weird way actually bolstered American soft power because when they published all these diplomatic cables, I know a lot... The global reaction was, “Oh, it turns out that a lot of times what they’re saying in these cables are actually what they are saying in public.” And they were making relatively shrewd observations about different human rights records or different leaders or so on and so forth. So there are times where weirdly the technology can aid soft power as well.DAN KURTZ-PHELANI mean, I was working in the State Department at the time of WikiLeaks, and we were of course panicked that it had all kinds of terrible consequences and it did have some, but by and large, the reaction was that some of these people are smarter than we though and have deeper insight and better information than we thought, which was striking.DANIEL DREZNERI had a Pakistani student, I still remember this when the WikiLeaks broke out, actually asked me if Julian Assange was a CIA agent because it worked so well for the United States. He’s like, “This is surely a CIA plot, right?” I’m like, “We’re not that good.”DAN KURTZ-PHELANElizabeth, you talked about the politics of this, and one thing that I think will be very dominant in Democratic debates about foreign policy will be frankly less Trump and more about Biden and Gaza and the extent to which that puts the lie to any kind of claims of exceptionalism or supporting human rights or democracy. I suppose a way of getting this is what’s the right way of having that kind of conversation with the party? You think a lot about how policy comes out of those debates and the way that that happens in a healthy and constructive way. So how would you like to see that debate happening and what do you think would set it off course or make it less likely to yield the right kind of outcome?ELIZABETH SAUNDERSYeah, I think about this a lot because I am sympathetic to those who want to have a blanket ban on anybody who worked on Gaza. Chris Van Hollen has said this in print and he’s now running for leadership that nobody who worked on Biden Middle East policy, or I forget what his exact parameters were, but essentially Gaza policy should be welcome back into a future Democratic administration.DAN KURTZ-PHELANAnd he could be Senate majority leader.ELIZABETH SAUNDERSYeah, exactly. He’s challenging Schumer for majority leader on many different grounds, but he has said that in print. So I am sympathetic to that argument, but I think the more productive thing... One thing that I do worry about is the several decades of populist anti-expertise rhetoric that has made serving in government or serving in a position that requires a lot of expertise in a public servant kind of a way, very unattractive. And I don’t mean this in a sort of elitist way, like we need to have our wonderful elites and let them make a lot of money. But I think what we’ve also experienced this week with all of these, the FAA outages, Microsoft, JP Morgan, I can’t remember what all the other ones were. Oh, the National Security Agency just yesterday, their classified system went down. We are being reminded every day that we need expertise and we can’t go without it, and how are we going to rebuild that at the same time that we are making sort of blanket bans on any topic worries me a little.I think the more productive way to get at this in a policy sense that might have the same effect is to have an intra-party debate. I am not of a mind that it should be taboo to have these debates within a party. I think it’s very healthy to have debates about aid to Israel, should we have these people back? I think if you had that debate productively, if it came out that people side with what Biden did in Gaza was wrong, the effect would be the same. You probably wouldn’t hire back the people who were very, very prominently making those decisions, but you wouldn’t do it via a blanket ban that might have all kinds of other effects on other issues and the staffing on other issues.DANIEL DREZNERI would just add two points on this. The first is that really one of the fundamental debates I think you’re going to see happen in 2028, and one of the recognitions that we need to have has been one of the things that the Trump administration... And it’s building on some things that have happened before, but this second term in particular has been quite acute, has been the erosion of U.S. state capacity, particularly in the area of foreign policy. USAID as an agency doesn’t exist anymore. You’ve eliminated a lot of ways in which you can provide carrots. The idea of actually negotiating trade deals by and large has been radically diminished. The diplomatic core has been gutted. The general officer core has also faced a severe retrenchment. Same with sort of high level civil servants across the board. There really is going to need to be a conversation about how you can actually rebuild some of this capacity.Regardless of ideology, you just want the state to be able to do certain things. And to Elizabeth’s point, the very fact that we had the FAA ground stop, this affects domestic policy as well as international policy. But again, it’s worth noting another component of Joe Nye’s soft power was the perception of policy competence. The U.S. has completely lost the perception of policy competence both domestically and internationally, and that’s something that we need to rebuild. The second thing that I think is true is that on the foreign policy elite side, on the sort of more political appointee advisor side that Elizabeth was referring to, it’s going to be a really interesting test of whether or not there is something called “the Blob” or not.
